items.label: f02-order-snapshots
items.front: Why does an order item copy the product name, SKU and unit price?
items.back: Later catalogue edits must not rewrite what the customer ordered. The product reference stays for inventory restoration; the snapshot preserves the original commercial description.

items.label: f03-archive-not-delete
items.front: An admin tries to delete a product that appears in past orders. What happens and why?
items.back: 409: deleteMany requires orderItems: none, because history and cancellation still reference the product. Archive it instead, which hides it from new purchases but keeps the row.

items.label: f01-three-identities
items.front: Customer identity, record version, retry identity: what does each answer at checkout?
items.back: Token subject: who is acting (never a submitted userId). Record version: which accepted state an editor started from (conditional writes). Checkout key: which logical create attempt, stored durably per customer, so a retry after an uncertain response returns the same order.

items.label: f04-payment-timeout
items.front: A payment provider call times out. Is it safe to charge again?
items.back: No: a timeout can mean rejection, no contact, or acceptance without a delivered response. Persist the payment intent first, use a stable provider idempotency key, record observed outcomes, and reconcile; webhooks need signature checks, dedup and an allowed-transition policy.

items.prompt: The same customer reuses a checkout key but adds an item to the cart. What happens?

choices.text: A new order is created under a regenerated key

The old order is returned, since the key matches
The new item is appended to the existing order

items.explanation: Returning the old receipt for a different request would be a silent wrong answer; the fingerprint is computed over sortedItems so line order does not matter.

items.prompt: Why is the checkout requestId lower-cased during parsing?

choices.text: It feeds both the advisory-lock key and the receipt lookup; if either used the raw spelling, two casings of one UUID could pass the lock separately
PostgreSQL rejects upper-case UUIDs
Because hashtextextended is case-insensitive anyway
To make the key look consistent in the admin UI

Read 1 stops locking others' orders; read 2 sees the state after the lock
The second read is redundant and exists only so the audit row can record the order's status

It returns the order as CANCELLED and reserves no stock
409, because cancelled orders cannot be replayed
The cancelled order is reopened as PENDING and stock is reserved again

items.prompt: Why does a popular product's admin edit history disappear after a few dozen orders?

choices.text: Audit events older than 30 days are deleted by a nightly retention job
Each checkout overwrites the previous audit row for that product instead of inserting a new one
Only the newest 30 events are returned, and each order adds RESERVE/RESTORE events
Edits are not audited at all; only orders are

items.explanation: Order history has the same limit but an order has at most four events, so only product history is a practical problem.

choices.text: To make the cheapest product reserve first
Because PostgreSQL requires FOR UPDATE locks in primary-key order
Two multi-product checkouts then acquire product locks in a common order, removing the circular wait that unsorted locking would reintroduce as a deadlock risk
So the receipt shows items alphabetically

items.prompt: A customer double-clicks Cancel, sending two cancellations with the same version. Why can stock not be restored twice?

choices.text: Both lock the order; the second sees a changed version (or status CANCELLED, which has no transitions) and conflicts before restoring anything
The second cancellation restores stock but a nightly job corrects it
Stock restoration is idempotent because it sets stock to an absolute value
The frontend disables the button, which is the only guard
